name: The Canterbury Tales
info: The Canterbury Tales is an anthology of twenty-four short stories, mostly in verse, written in Middle English by Geoffrey Chaucer between 1387 and 1400 and told by pilgrims travelling from London to Becket's shrine at Canterbury.

facts.made: Geoffrey Chaucer, who wrote it between 1387 and 1400 while serving as Controller of Customs, Justice of the Peace and Clerk of the King's Works; copied by scribes, among them one identified as Adam Pinkhurst
facts.form: An anthology of twenty-four tales in Middle English, mostly in verse with five stressed syllables to the line, set within a frame tale of pilgrims; Sir Thopas and the prose tales differ in metre, and four tales use rhyme royal
facts.where: No manuscript in Chaucer's own hand survives; 84 manuscripts and four incunabula editions are known, including William Caxton's 1476 edition, of which ten copies survive, among them one at the British Library and one at the Folger Shakespeare Library
facts.known: The General Prologue's portraits of the pilgrims; the storytelling contest; the Knight's Tale and the Miller's interruption; the Pardoner and the Summoner; the Wife of Bath; the pilgrimage to Saint Thomas Becket's shrine; the Middle English of a London dialect; its incompleteness

t: Chaucer set a collection of tales inside a pilgrimage, a framework no earlier work is known to have used, and let the pilgrims' classes, occupations and views shape the stories they tell.
He planned about 120 stories, four from each of some 30 pilgrims, but most scholars think the work was incomplete at the end of his life, and there is no consensus on its intended order.
No manuscript in Chaucer's hand survives; the text comes from 84 manuscripts and four incunabula, and later writers added tales and prologues to fill its gaps.
dyk: The Canterbury Tales survives in more manuscripts than any other vernacular English literary text except Prick of Conscience, yet Derek Pearsall cautions that this should not be taken as proof of its popularity in the century after Chaucer's death.
ev: Chaucer begins writing The Canterbury Tales, a work he continues until 1400
The period of composition ends with the Tales incomplete, as most scholars think
John Lydgate writes The Siege of Thebes, which places himself among the pilgrims
William Caxton prints the first edition of the Tales
John Stow prints Lydgate's Siege of Thebes
John Urry's edition prints the Tale of Beryn alongside the Tales
F. J. Furnivall identifies nine Groups of tales under the auspices of the Chaucer Society
Following John M. Manly and Edith Rickert, scholars increasingly favour the Hengwrt manuscript over Ellesmere

sections.origins:
The Canterbury Tales was written between 1387 and 1400. In 1386 Chaucer became Controller of Customs and Justice of the Peace, and in 1389 Clerk of the King's Works; it was during these years that he began working on the Tales. The end of the fourteenth century was a turbulent time in English history. The Catholic Church was in the midst of the Western Schism and, although it was still the only Christian authority in Western Europe, it was the subject of heavy controversy. The Peasants' Revolt of 1381 and the clashes that ended in the deposing of King Richard II belong to the same turmoil, and many of Chaucer's close friends were executed, while he himself moved to Kent to get away from events in London.

No other work before Chaucer's is known to have set a collection of tales within the framework of pilgrims on a pilgrimage. Storytelling was the main entertainment in England at the time, and storytelling contests had been around for hundreds of years. In 14th-century England the English Pui was a group with an appointed leader who judged the songs of the group; the winner received a crown and, as with the winner of the Tales, a free dinner. It was common for pilgrims to choose a master of ceremonies to guide them and organise the journey. Harold Bloom suggests that the structure is mostly original but inspired by the pilgrim figures of Dante and Virgil in The Divine Comedy.
sections.content:
The Tales are presented as part of a fictional storytelling contest held by a group of pilgrims travelling from London to Canterbury to visit the shrine of Saint Thomas Becket at Canterbury Cathedral. In the General Prologue some 30 pilgrims are introduced. According to the Prologue, Chaucer intended four stories from each pilgrim, two on the way to the shrine and two on the way back, about 120 in all. The frame is a common and long established genre, but Chaucer's collection differs from most others in its intense variation: most story collections kept to a theme, usually a religious one, while here the structure depends on the characters.

The Knight tells the first tale, which suggests that the pilgrims will speak by class, with the Monk to follow. The Miller then interrupts with his own tale, and the structure gives way to an open exchange among all classes present. The characters are divided into three estates: those who pray, those who fight and those who work. Two tales, Sir Topas and The Tale of Melibee, are told by Chaucer himself, who travels with the pilgrims in his own story. Religion is a major theme. The Pardoner and the Summoner are portrayed as deeply corrupt, greedy and abusive, and the Monk and the Prioress fall short of the ideal for their orders. The Prioress's Tale is an account of Jews murdering a pious Christian boy, a blood libel that became part of English literary tradition; the story did not originate with Chaucer and was well known in the 14th century.
sections.making:
Chaucer wrote mainly in a London dialect of late Middle English. He pronounced the -e at the end of many words, and other letters now silent were also sounded; the Great Vowel Shift had not yet happened. Because the final -e was lost soon after his time, scribes did not copy it accurately, which gave scholars the impression that Chaucer was inconsistent in using it. It has now been established that the -e was an important part of his grammar, distinguishing singular adjectives from plural and subjunctive verbs from indicative. He used one metre in almost all the tales, a line with five stressed syllables, usually of ten syllables, which was probably inspired by French and Italian forms and is an ancestor of iambic pentameter. Four tales, the Man of Law's, Clerk's, Prioress's and Second Nun's, use rhyme royal.

Chaucer borrowed portions, sometimes very large portions, of his stories from earlier works. A quarter of the tales parallel a tale in the Decameron of Giovanni Boccaccio, though most have closer parallels elsewhere, and some scholars think he merely read it, perhaps during his first diplomatic mission to Italy in 1372. He drew often on the Bible, Ovid, Petrarch, Dante, Boethius' Consolation of Philosophy and his friend John Gower, and on religious works such as John Bromyard's Summa praedicantium. New research suggests that the General Prologue is a pastiche of Harry Bailey's surviving 1381 poll-tax account of Southwark's inhabitants.
sections.reception:
The intended audience of the Tales is hard to determine. Chaucer was a courtier, which leads some to believe that he wrote mainly for the nobility, and Eustache Deschamps and his contemporary John Gower called him a noble translator and poet. The poem may have been meant to be read aloud, as was a common activity then, but it also seems intended for private reading, since Chaucer often refers to himself as the writer rather than the speaker. Scholars speculate that manuscripts circulated among his friends in his lifetime but were unknown to most people until after his death. The speed with which copyists strove to write complete versions suggests that he was a famous and respected poet in his own day.

John Lydgate and Thomas Occleve were among the first critics of the Tales. They praised Chaucer as the greatest English poet and the first to show what the language could do, a view later critics shared into the mid-15th century. Glosses in manuscripts of the time praised his skill with sentence and rhetoric, the two pillars by which medieval critics judged poetry, and the most respected tale was then the Knight's. Even the most elegant illustrated manuscript, however, is not nearly as highly decorated as the work of authors of more respectable works such as Lydgate's religious and historical writing.
sections.survival:
There are 84 manuscripts and four incunabula editions of the work, printed before 1500. Fifty-five manuscripts are thought to have been originally complete, while 28 are so fragmentary that it is hard to tell whether they were copied singly or as part of a set. The Tales vary from manuscript to manuscript. Many minor variations are due to copyists' errors, though research is divided over whether these were errors or the copyists' own changes, and in other cases Chaucer may have added to his work and revised it as it was being copied. The two earliest known manuscripts, both apparently copied by one scribe, are the Hengwrt manuscript and the Ellesmere Manuscript, a deluxe, illustrated copy. The scribe has been identified as Adam Pinkhurst, an identification that has been much disputed in Middle English palaeography, though widely accepted as plausible. Until the 1940s scholars tended to prefer Ellesmere, but following John M. Manly and Edith Rickert they increasingly favoured Hengwrt.

The first printed version was William Caxton's 1476 edition, one of the first books he printed; only ten copies are known. Order remains unsettled. Editions divide the Tales into ten Fragments, following the Ellesmere order, and the Victorian Furnivall's nine Groups, used for most of the twentieth century in Skeat's edition for Oxford University Press, are seldom followed today.
sections.legacy:
The Canterbury Tales are widely regarded as Chaucer's magnum opus and are revered as one of the paramount works of English literature. They had a major effect on the development of English literature and may have helped to popularise the English vernacular in mainstream literature, as opposed to French or Latin. Their incompleteness led medieval authors to write additions: expansions of the Cook's Tale, which Chaucer never finished, The Plowman's Tale, The Tale of Gamelyn, the Tale of Beryn and Lydgate's Siege of Thebes. The Tale of Gamelyn, found in the poor-quality Harley 7334 manuscript, is now widely rejected by scholars as Chaucer's own.

Later writers kept returning to the frame. The Two Noble Kinsmen, by William Shakespeare and John Fletcher, retells the Knight's Tale and was first performed in 1613 or 1614. Harriet Lee's The Canterbury Tales, of twelve stories told by travellers thrown together by accident, influenced Lord Byron. Erik Chisholm completed an opera in 1961, and Nevill Coghill's modern English version was the basis of a musical staged in 1964. Dan Simmons based his 1989 novel Hyperion on a group of pilgrims, Richard Dawkins used the structure for The Ancestor's Tale in 2004, and Refugee Tales, a collabouration of writers and displaced people, models its stories on Chaucer's journey. In 2021 Zadie Smith adapted the Wife of Bath's Prologue and Tale in The Wife of Willesden.

summary: The Canterbury Tales is Chaucer's anthology of twenty-four tales in Middle English, told by pilgrims travelling to Becket's shrine at Canterbury. Written between 1387 and 1400 and probably unfinished, it survives in 84 manuscripts and was first printed by Caxton in 1476.
